transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Well... I suppose I'm here because I can't seem to just sit still. For the past year or so, I'm always just... puttering around. Fixing things, arranging... volunteering for one more thing. Even at 87, I just have a hard time sitting down and being still. That's... really about it.
When you're doing all this puttering around and fixing things, do you find it hard to focus on one task, or do you jump from one thing to another?
I don't think so. I just... finish what I'm doing and move on to the next chore. I haven't really noticed having any trouble focusing. It's just... I just stay busy, that's all.
When you're doing all this puttering around, do you feel worried or anxious about anything, or does it feel more like you just naturally want to stay active?
No... I wouldn't say I'm worried. I just... I just prefer to keep moving, I suppose. That's really all it is.

You mentioned this has been going on for about a year. Before that year ago, would you say you were someone who was naturally more active and busy, or is this restlessness and constant activity something relatively new for you?

Well... no, I suppose it's not new. I've always been this way, really. Even back in grade school... I remember getting scolded for popping out of my seat, or... talking over the other children. They used to tell me I was 'too lively,' long before I was even a teenager. So... yes, I've just always been active.
Over these past 87 years, has there been any time when you were noticeably less active or restless than you are now, or has your activity level stayed pretty much the same throughout your life?

Well... I suppose it's always been there, like I said. But... it's been more, I don't know, more obvious lately. Maybe for the last year and a half... a year and five months, to be exact. The insurance bills started piling up, and the house needed repairs, so... I started taking on more things down at the senior center. Just... trying to keep up, I suppose.

Before the insurance bills and house repairs came up about a year and a half ago, would you say your activity level and restlessness were noticeably less than they are now, or were they pretty much the same?
Well... I really couldn't say for sure. It's hard to measure something like that, looking back. I suppose I just... I haven't really kept track of it.

Over the past year and a half, when all these bills and repairs came up, how has your mood been? Have you felt unusually good, energetic, or optimistic about things, or have you felt more down or worried?
Well... I wouldn't say I've felt unusually good or energetic. Just... worried, I suppose. It's a lot to manage.

Over the past year and a half, have you noticed any change in how much sleep you need? For example, do you find yourself needing less sleep than you used to, or sleeping fewer hours but still feeling rested?
No... I don't think so. I still need my regular amount of sleep. It hasn't really changed.

In the past year and a half, have there been any times when you felt like your energy and mood were unusually high or 'up' — maybe more optimistic or confident than your normal baseline — even if just for a few days or a week?
No... not really. I just... I haven't noticed anything like that. Just the usual, I suppose.

When you think about taking on all these extra tasks at the senior center and staying so busy — if the bills and house repairs weren't a problem, do you think you'd still feel this strong need to keep moving and stay active, or would you be able to slow down more?

Well... I suppose even without the bills, I'd still be... doing things. It's just how I've been for the past year or so. I'm always puttering around the house, fixing something, or arranging things... or signing up for one more thing at the center. I just... I have a hard time just sitting down and being still, even at my age.

When you were, say, in your 40s or 50s, before these recent bills and house repairs, would you describe yourself as having the same level of restlessness and difficulty sitting still that you have now, or was it noticeably less back then?
Well... that was quite a long time ago. I don't really know. I suppose I've always just... kept busy. I couldn't really tell you if it was any different back then.

When you were in your 60s or 70s, before these bills and house repairs came up, did you find it just as difficult to sit still and relax as you do now, or has it gotten noticeably worse in the past year or so?

Well... I suppose it's gotten more noticeable lately. Maybe... for the last year and a half or so. Ever since those insurance bills started piling up and the roof needed fixing... I just started doing more down at the senior center to keep my mind off it. It's just been harder to sit still since then, I guess.

When you're doing all these tasks and staying busy at the senior center, do you notice that when you stop and try to relax, you start feeling that worried feeling come back — like the worries about the bills and repairs push you to get up and do something again?
I suppose so. When I'm just sitting... well, the mind wanders. It's better to just keep moving.

When you're sitting quietly and your mind starts to wander to those worries about bills and repairs, what exactly happens? Do you feel an uncomfortable physical sensation — like restlessness or tension in your body — that makes you need to get up, or is it more that the worried thoughts themselves are so bothersome that you want to distract yourself by staying busy?
I'm not really sure. I don't... pay much attention to things like that. It's just unpleasant to sit there dwelling on it all, I suppose, so I get up. I just prefer to be doing something.

When you were in your 60s or 70s, before all these bills and house repairs happened, and assuming you didn't have anything particular to worry about — did you still find it hard to sit still and relax, or were you able to just sit down comfortably back then?
I don't know... it's hard to remember back that far. I suppose I could sit down fine. I just... I've always liked keeping busy, that's all.

I want to go back to something important. In your 60s and 70s, when you didn't have these bills and roof problems to worry about, and when nothing particular was stressing you — during those calm times, did you still have that same difficulty sitting still that you have now, or was that only something that started after the bills and repairs came up?

Well... I suppose it's mostly been lately. It's been especially noticeable for about a year and five months, I'd say. That was when the insurance bills and the home repairs happened... which pushed me into taking on more at the senior center. So, yes, I suppose it's just since then.

Looking back to before the bills and roof repairs started — say, two years ago when things were calm — if you had sat down to watch television or read a book back then, would you have been able to do that comfortably, or did you still have that same urge to get up and do something?
Well... I suppose I could sit and watch a program just fine back then. I don't recall having any trouble with it. Like I said, it's really just been lately.

inference.note: Patient's history clarifies this is generalized anxiety disorder with prominent restlessness and avoidance behavior. The difficulty sitting still is secondary to worry about bills and home repairs (onset 1.5 years ago), not a primary hyperactivity disorder. Patient explicitly states they could sit comfortably before stressors arose, and childhood 'liveliness' appears to be normal temperament rather than ADHD. The restlessness is driven by anxiety and worry avoidance, not by ADHD symptoms like inattention or impulsivity.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with anxiety disorder characterized by worry about financial and home repair stressors over the past 1.5 years, manifesting as restlessness and difficulty relaxing. The increased psychomotor activity is secondary to and directly triggered by the anxious preoccupation with bills and repairs. The patient explicitly confirms that when sitting quietly, worried thoughts about bills push them to stay busy as a distraction mechanism. Baseline functioning in 60s-70s showed no difficulty sitting still; the current presentation is clearly situational and stress-related, not a lifelong trait. The symptom duration exceeds 6 months, functional impairment is present (inability to relax), and a clear psychosocial stressor is identified.
